what_it_is: A repository, generation pipeline and benchmark for LLMs' physical commonsense about everyday objects. Crowd workers rated 700+ household object categories on eight qualitative attributes (e.g. elasticity, brittleness, sharpness) on a 3-point scale, at least four ratings per pair and over 20,000 in all, kept only at 75% agreement (pp. 2-3). Templates filled from this repository give 160K multiple-choice and true/false questions in three tracks: attribute comprehension, explicit comparison and implicit scenario-based choice (pp. 2, 4). Ten models, from Flan-T5 to GPT-4, are scored by agreement with the human majority or by accuracy; GPT-4's attribute agreement is 49.7% against 84.4% among humans (Table 4, p. 6).
domain: physical commonsense: qualitative attributes of everyday household objects, motivated by robotic manipulation (pp. 1-2)
size: 160K questions over 700+ objects and 8 attributes (2,800 object-attribute pairs); 10 models in Track 1 (pp. 1, 4, 6)
source_of_items: generated from templates: object categories from 3D-object datasets mapped to WordNet, attribute labels crowd-sourced; the Track 3 scenarios are hand-designed (pp. 2-4, 11)
instances: generated (template-filled from the repository; the 160K set is pre-generated, and the pipeline can produce customised variants) (pp. 1-3)
evaluation: multiple choice and true/false: agreement with the human majority weighted by human agreement (Track 1), accuracy (Tracks 2 and 3) (p. 5; appendix A.1, p. 11)
human_validation: Every object-attribute pair was rated by at least four crowd annotators (20,000+ annotations) and kept only at agreement of at least 0.75 with an extreme rating (pp. 2-3); human inter-annotator agreement averages 84.4% (Table 4, p. 6). The authors note that crowd labels may still contain errors (p. 9).

engtrace_use.sentence: S-P1: 'While UGPhysics (Xu et al., 2025) and PhysReason (Zhang et al., 2025a) effectively test the application of reasoning to natural laws, others target advanced symbolic (Zhang et al., 2025b; Qiu et al., 2025) or qualitative (Wang et al., 2023; Shojaee et al., 2025) understanding.' S-P2: 'Despite this progress, these benchmarks remain confined to theoretical physics, lacking the integrative context of engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: S-P1's 'qualitative understanding' is accurate: NEWTON tests qualitative attributes of everyday objects, not calculation (pp. 1-2, 4). S-P2 then says all six cited benchmarks 'remain confined to theoretical physics', which is false for NEWTON: it concerns physical commonsense about household objects, motivated by robotic manipulation (pp. 1-2, 8), and contains no physics theory. The May text also omits that NEWTON's questions are generated from templates (pp. 1-3), a precedent the Introduction's account of symbolic templates as EngTrace's generative mechanism should not overlook. In short, S-P1 is accurate and S-P2 is wrong for this paper.

suggested_wording: NEWTON (Wang et al., 2023) instead probes qualitative physical commonsense, generating 160K multiple-choice and true/false questions from templates over crowd-sourced attribute labels for 700+ everyday objects.
facts_to_cite: It covers eight qualitative attributes (e.g. elasticity, brittleness, sharpness) of 700+ everyday object categories, rated by crowd workers, at least four per pair (pp. 2-3).
Its 160K questions are generated from templates, in three tracks: attribute comprehension, explicit application and implicit scenario-based analysis (pp. 2, 4).
The questions are multiple choice or true/false (p. 4).
GPT-4 agrees with the human majority on 49.7% of attribute questions, against 84.4% agreement among humans (Table 4, p. 6), but averages 87.7% on the scenario track (p. 6).
It is motivated by LLMs in physically grounded settings such as robotic manipulation (p. 1).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: template-based generation of test items from a curated repository (pp. 1-3), and human labels with an agreement filter. Lacks: quantitative multi-step problems, gold traces, step-level evaluation (multiple choice and true/false only), engineering domain, and any contamination analysis.
notes: The object count is 700+ in the text (pp. 2, 4) but '600+' in Table 2 (p. 5). The May reference list prints 'Jia Duan' for Jiafei Duan (p. 1) and gives arXiv rather than Findings of EMNLP 2023. Key clash: the July rebuttal cites SciBench as 'Wang et al., 2023', the key that denotes NEWTON in the May reference list. NEWTON is peripheral to EngTrace's positioning; of the six physics citations it is the cheapest to cut if space is short.
